commands.title: Update & upgrade all packages
commands.description: Updates the package list and upgrades everything to the latest version. Run this first on any fresh Termux install. Run immediately after installing Termux. Press Enter to keep defaults when prompted. 💡 If asked about config file changes during upgrade, press Enter to keep the installed version. Very first command on a new install, and periodically to keep tools updated and secure.

commands.title: Grant storage permission
commands.description: Requests access to Android's internal storage. Creates ~/storage/ with shortcuts to Downloads, DCIM, Music, etc. Run once → tap "Allow" in the popup. Access files at ~/storage/shared/ or ~/storage/downloads/ Once after fresh install. Required to share files between Termux, Acode, and your file manager.

commands.title: Install the full dev toolkit
commands.command: pkg install git nodejs python openssh curl wget nano zip unzip -y
commands.description: Installs Git, Node.js/npm, Python, SSH, curl, wget, nano, zip, and unzip in one shot. Your complete baseline stack. One-time setup on a fresh Termux. After this you can do web dev, scripting, and version control immediately.

commands.title: Create your dev workspace
commands.description: Creates an organized workspace and navigates into it. All your projects should live here for consistency. After initial Termux setup. Every new project and git clone should land under ~/dev/projects/

commands.title: Show Termux environment info
commands.description: Displays Termux version, Android version, CPU architecture, and installed package count. Troubleshooting, reporting bugs, or verifying your environment before starting a project.

commands.title: List all installed packages
commands.description: Lists every package currently installed in your Termux environment with its installed version. Auditing your environment or checking if a specific tool is already installed before reinstalling. Install, remove, search, and manage all software in Termux using the pkg command — a friendly wrapper around apt.

commands.title: Install a package
commands.description: Installs any available package. -y auto-confirms all prompts without interaction. "Replace package-name: git, nodejs, python, vim, ffmpeg, mariadb, php, etc." Every time you need a new tool, language runtime, or CLI in Termux.

commands.title: Remove a package
commands.description: Removes an installed package from Termux, freeing storage space on your device. When you no longer need a tool — especially useful on phones with limited storage.

commands.title: Search for a package
commands.description: Searches the available package repo for matching names or keywords. Partial names work fine. "Try: pkg search java | pkg search http | pkg search image" When you don't know the exact package name or want to discover available tools. Move around the filesystem and manage directories with professional efficiency.

commands.title: Go to home directory
commands.description: Returns to Termux home (/data/data/com.termux/files/home). The ~ always refers to home. When lost deep in directories and need to return to your base. Plain "cd" works too.

commands.title: List files with full details
commands.description: Lists all files including hidden ones, with permissions, human-readable sizes, and timestamps. The most informative listing format. ls = simple. ls -la = detailed + hidden. ls -lah = detailed + human sizes. ls -lt = sorted by time. Before any operation on a folder — always check what's actually there first.

commands.title: Print current directory path
commands.description: Prints the full absolute path of your current location. Removes all ambiguity about where you are. Before running any destructive command. Also useful for copying the current path.

commands.title: Create nested project structure
commands.description: Creates a project folder with multiple subdirectories using brace expansion. One command, full structure. Scaffolding a new project without a framework CLI — create the entire directory tree instantly.

commands.title: Remove a folder and all contents
commands.description: Permanently deletes a folder and everything inside it. Irreversible — no recycle bin in Termux. Always confirm with pwd and ls first. Never run rm -rf ~ or rm -rf / ⚠️ Double-check the name before pressing Enter. This permanently deletes everything inside. Deleting node_modules, old build dirs, or entire project folders you no longer need. Create, copy, move, rename, and delete files. The everyday operations you'll run on every project.

commands.title: Create empty files
commands.description: Creates one or more empty files at once. If a file already exists, updates its timestamp without changing content. Starting any new component, config file, or script you'll edit in Acode right after.

commands.title: Create a file with content
commands.description: Creates a file and writes text into it. > overwrites. >> appends to an existing file without overwriting. echo "text" > file — create/overwrite. echo "text" >> file — append a line. Seeding config files, adding lines to .env, or writing a quick script stub from the terminal.

commands.title: Copy a file or directory
commands.command: cp source.js destination.js cp -r src/ src-backup/
commands.description: Copies files or entire directories. -r is required for directories. cp .env.example .env — copy a template to create your local config file. Creating backups, duplicating files, or copying templates before editing.

commands.title: Move or rename a file
commands.command: mv old-name.js new-name.js mv component.jsx src/components/
commands.description: Moves a file to a new path or renames it. Works for both files and directories. Refactoring project structure, renaming components, or reorganizing files during development.

commands.title: Delete a file
commands.command: rm filename.js rm -i filename.js # with confirmation prompt
commands.description: Permanently deletes a file. Cannot be undone — Termux has no recycle bin. Use -i for a confirmation prompt. Removing old files, generated artifacts, or temporary files no longer needed in your project. Read file contents, inspect logs, count lines, search text, and check disk usage from the terminal.

commands.title: Print full file contents
commands.description: Outputs a file's entire contents to the terminal. Best for short files — configs, .env, package.json, .gitignore. Quick checks on small files. For large files use head, tail, or less instead to avoid flooding the terminal.

commands.title: View first N lines
commands.description: Shows only the first N lines. Default is 10. Ideal for previewing large files or log headers without loading everything. Checking file structure, import headers, or the first entries of a large log file.

commands.title: View last N lines + follow mode
commands.command: tail -50 app.log # Live follow — shows new lines as written: tail -f app.log
commands.description: Shows the last N lines. -f follows the file in real-time — essential for monitoring live server logs. Press Ctrl+C to stop. Monitoring a running server, reading error logs, or watching a build process output live.

commands.title: Search text inside files (grep)
commands.command: grep -rn \"TODO\" ./src grep -ri \"console.log\" . # case-insensitive grep -rl \"import React\" . # filenames only
commands.description: Recursively searches all files for a string. -r = recursive, -n = line numbers, -i = case-insensitive, -l = filenames only. Finding all TODOs, tracking function usage, auditing console.logs before a production push.

commands.title: Count lines / words / bytes
commands.command: wc -l filename.js wc -l src/*.js # multiple files with total
commands.description: "-l counts lines, -w counts words, -c counts bytes. Works on multiple files and shows a grand total." Checking file sizes, counting rows in a dataset, or seeing how large your codebase has grown.

commands.title: Install Termux
commands.command: # Download Termux from F-Droid (NOT Google Play)
commands.description: Termux is a terminal emulator for Android. The Google Play version is outdated — always install from F-Droid (f-droid.org) or GitHub releases. 1. Open your browser → go to f-droid.org 2. Search 'Termux' → Download and install 3. Open Termux → it will set up its environment automatically This is the very first step before doing anything with Git on Android.

commands.title: Install Acode Editor
commands.command: # Download Acode from Google Play Store
commands.description: Acode is a powerful code editor for Android with syntax highlighting, file management, and FTP support. It's your 'VS Code' on Android. 1. Open Google Play Store 2. Search 'Acode - code editor' 3. Install and open it 4. Give it storage permissions when asked Install this alongside Termux so you can edit code files with a proper code editor.

commands.title: Update Termux packages
commands.description: Updates all pre-installed Termux packages to the latest versions. Always do this first after installing Termux. Open Termux → paste this command → press Enter → wait for it to finish. 💡 If asked to choose a configuration, just press Enter to keep the default. Run this immediately after installing Termux, and periodically to stay updated.

commands.title: Install Git in Termux
commands.description: Installs Git version control in Termux. Without this, no Git commands will work. Paste the command in Termux and press Enter. It will download and install Git. Run once after updating Termux packages.

commands.title: Install essential tools
commands.command: pkg install openssh curl wget nano -y
commands.description: Installs SSH (for GitHub auth), curl & wget (for downloads), and nano (a simple text editor). Paste and run. These will be available immediately after installation. Right after installing Git — these tools are needed for most Git workflows.

commands.title: Install Node.js (optional)
commands.description: Installs Node.js and npm for JavaScript/TypeScript development. Optional but useful for web projects. If you're working on web projects (React, Next.js, etc.).

commands.title: Install Python (optional)
commands.description: Installs Python 3 for Python development. Useful for scripting and automation. If you need Python for your projects or scripts.

commands.title: Grant Termux storage access
commands.description: Gives Termux access to your phone's shared storage (Downloads, Documents, etc.). Creates a ~/storage folder with symlinks. Run the command → tap 'Allow' when the permission popup appears. You'll see ~/storage/shared (your internal storage) and ~/storage/downloads. 💡 Your projects should live in ~/storage/shared/ so Acode can also access them. Run once so you can access files between Termux, Acode, and your file manager.

commands.title: Create a projects folder
commands.description: Creates a 'projects' folder in shared storage where both Termux and Acode can access your code. Run the command. From now on, always navigate here before cloning or creating repos. "💡 In Acode, open this folder: Internal Storage → projects" After granting storage access — this is where all your Git repos will live.

commands.title: Set Termux as Acode terminal
commands.command: # In Acode: Settings → App → Terminal → Choose Termux
commands.description: Links Acode to Termux so you can open a terminal directly from your code editor. 1. Open Acode 2. Go to Settings (gear icon) 3. Scroll to 'Terminal' 4. Select 'Termux' as the terminal app After installing both apps — makes your workflow much smoother.

commands.title: Verify Git installation
commands.description: Shows the installed Git version. If this works, Git is ready to use. Run in Termux. You should see something like 'git version 2.45.2'. After installing Git, to confirm it's working properly.

commands.title: Set your name
commands.description: Sets the author name that appears on every commit you make. Replace 'Your Name' with your actual name. Replace 'Your Name' with your real name or GitHub username, then run the command. This is the very first global config you must set.

commands.title: Set your email
commands.description: Sets the author email for your commits. This appears in the commit history and should match your GitHub email. Replace you@example.com with the email you use for GitHub. Right after setting your name. This pair completes your identity setup.

commands.title: Set default text editor
commands.description: "Sets the editor Git opens for commit messages. Options: nano (easy), vim (powerful), or any other available editor." Optional but saves time if you're uncomfortable with vim. nano is beginner-friendly.

commands.title: View all your Git config
commands.description: Shows every Git setting you've configured globally and for the current repo. Troubleshooting identity issues or confirming your settings were saved.

commands.title: Generate SSH key pair
commands.description: Creates a new SSH key for GitHub authentication. Ed25519 is the modern, secure standard. When prompted for location, just press Enter. When asked for passphrase, press Enter for no passphrase (easier on mobile). Once per device setup. Creates ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 (private) and ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub (public).

commands.title: Display your public SSH key
commands.description: Prints your public key. Copy this entire output and paste it into GitHub settings. Highlight all output → long-press → Copy. Then go to GitHub Settings → SSH and GPG keys → Add new. After generating your key, before attempting any SSH connection to GitHub.

commands.title: Initialize a new repository
commands.description: Creates a .git folder, turning your current directory into a Git repository. cd into your project folder, then run this command. Creating a brand new local project before first commit.

commands.title: Set default branch to main
commands.description: Makes 'main' the default branch name for new repos. The older default was 'master' — 'main' is the modern standard. Run once during initial setup. All new repos you create will start with 'main'.

commands.title: Set nano as default editor
commands.description: Sets nano as the editor Git opens for commit messages, rebases, etc. Nano is beginner-friendly and works great in Termux. After running this, when Git asks you to edit a message, nano will open instead of vim. Run once. In Termux, nano is much easier than vim (the default). 💡

commands.title: Enable colorful output
commands.description: Makes Git output colorful — added lines in green, removed in red, branch names highlighted. Easier to read. Run once during setup. Makes all Git output much more readable.

commands.title: Set pull to rebase
commands.description: When you pull, your local commits get replayed on top of remote changes instead of creating ugly merge commits. Set once if you want a cleaner, linear commit history. 💡

commands.title: Set push to current branch
commands.description: When you run 'git push', it automatically pushes the current branch to a same-named branch on the remote. Set once — saves you from typing the branch name every time you push.

commands.title: Enable credential caching
commands.description: Caches your GitHub username/password (or token) for 1 hour so you don't have to re-enter it every push/pull. Run this once. Next time you enter credentials, they'll be cached for 3600 seconds (1 hour). If you use HTTPS URLs for repos and get tired of entering credentials.

commands.title: List all your config
commands.description: Shows every Git setting and which file it comes from (system, global, or local). Great for debugging. When something isn't working right, or to verify your setup is correct.

commands.title: Check a specific setting
commands.description: Shows the current value of a specific config setting. Replace user.name with any setting name. To quickly verify one specific setting without listing everything.

commands.title: Create a .gitignore
commands.description: Creates a .gitignore file that tells Git which files to ignore (not track). Essential for keeping junk out of your repo. Run inside your project folder. Edit the file to add more patterns as needed. At the start of every new project, before your first commit. 💡 Set up SSH keys for secure, password-free authentication with GitHub. No more typing passwords on every push!

commands.title: Generate SSH key
commands.description: Creates a modern Ed25519 SSH key pair. This is like a digital ID card that proves you are you — without passwords. 1. Replace the email with yours 2. Run the command 3. Press Enter 3 times (accept default location, no passphrase for Termux) 4. Your key is created! Once per device, before you can push/pull using SSH URLs. 💡

commands.title: Display your public key
commands.description: Shows your public SSH key. You need to copy this and add it to GitHub. 1. Run the command 2. Long-press and copy the ENTIRE output (starts with 'ssh-ed25519') 3. Go to GitHub → Settings → SSH Keys → New SSH Key → paste it After generating your SSH key — to copy it to GitHub.

commands.title: Start SSH agent
commands.description: Starts the SSH agent (a helper that remembers your key) and adds your key to it. After generating your key, and each time you open Termux. 💡

commands.title: Test GitHub connection
commands.description: Tests if your SSH key works with GitHub. If successful, you'll see 'Hi username! You've successfully authenticated'. Run the command. If asked 'Are you sure you want to continue connecting?', type 'yes' and press Enter. After adding your public key to GitHub — to verify it works.

commands.title: Auto-start SSH agent
commands.description: Adds SSH agent startup to your shell config so it runs automatically when you open Termux. Once, after confirming SSH works — so you never have to manually start the agent.

commands.title: Fix SSH permissions
commands.description: Sets the correct file permissions for SSH files. SSH refuses to work if permissions are too open. "If you get 'WARNING: UNPROTECTED PRIVATE KEY FILE' or SSH connection fails."

commands.title: Initialize new repo
commands.description: Creates a new empty Git repository in the current folder. Adds a hidden .git directory that stores all version history. 1. cd into your project folder 2. Run 'git init' 3. You now have a Git repo! Start adding files. When starting a brand-new project from scratch.

commands.title: Init with main branch
commands.description: Same as git init, but explicitly names the first branch 'main'. Preferred over plain git init. On any new project — always use this over plain 'git init'. Track changes and save snapshots to history. Think of staging as 'selecting files for a photo' and committing as 'taking the photo'.

commands.title: Check status
commands.description: Shows which files are modified, staged, or untracked. This is your dashboard — it tells you what Git sees. Just run 'git status'. Red files = not staged. Green files = staged and ready to commit. ALL THE TIME. Before staging, before committing, when confused. This is your best friend. 💡

commands.title: Short status
commands.description: Compact, one-line-per-file status. Shows branch name at top. M = modified, A = added, ?? = untracked. When you want a quick glance without scrolling through verbose output.

commands.title: Stage a specific file
commands.description: Adds ONE specific file to the staging area. The staging area is like a 'shopping cart' for your next commit. Replace 'path/to/file.txt' with the actual file path shown in 'git status'. When you want to commit only specific files, not everything.

commands.title: Stage multiple files
commands.description: Stages multiple specific files at once. List them separated by spaces. When you want to commit a few specific files together.

commands.title: Stage everything
commands.description: Stages ALL changes in the current directory — new files, modified files, and deleted files. Run 'git add .' (note the dot!) then verify with 'git status'. When all your changes belong in the same commit. 💡

commands.title: Stage all tracked files
commands.description: Stages only modified and deleted files that Git already knows about. Does NOT add new untracked files. When you want to stage changes to existing files but not accidentally add new files.

commands.title: Stage interactively
commands.description: Goes through each change piece-by-piece and asks 'Stage this chunk? [y/n]'. Lets you split changes into multiple commits. "Run the command → for each chunk: y = stage, n = skip, q = quit." When a file has multiple unrelated changes that should be in separate commits.

commands.title: Commit with message
commands.description: Records all staged changes as a permanent snapshot with a descriptive message. This is like saving a checkpoint in a game. "Put your message in quotes after -m. Good format: \"type: what you did\"" After staging the files you want to save. Always write meaningful messages! 💡

commands.title: Stage + commit in one step
commands.description: Stages all MODIFIED tracked files and commits them in one command. Does NOT include new untracked files. Quick shortcut when all your changes are to files Git already knows about. 💡

commands.title: Amend last commit
commands.description: Adds your currently staged changes to the PREVIOUS commit without changing its message. Rewrites history! When you forgot to include a small change in your last commit. 💡

commands.title: Change last commit message
commands.description: Replaces the message of your most recent commit. When you spot a typo in your last commit message.

commands.title: Unstage a file
commands.description: Removes a file from the staging area but keeps your edits. Like taking something out of the shopping cart. Replace the path with the file shown in green in 'git status'. When you accidentally staged a file you didn't want in the next commit.

commands.title: Discard file changes
commands.description: "Reverts a file back to how it was in the last commit. WARNING: Your edits are permanently deleted!" When you messed up a file and want the last committed version back. 💡

commands.title: See what you changed
commands.description: Shows line-by-line what you changed in files that are NOT yet staged. Green = added, Red = removed. Before 'git add' — to review exactly what you changed.

commands.title: See what's staged
commands.description: Shows line-by-line what's in the staging area — what will go into the next commit. After 'git add', before 'git commit' — a final review. Branches let you work on features or fixes in isolation without breaking the main code. Think of them as parallel timelines.

commands.title: List local branches
commands.description: Shows all branches on your device. The current branch has a * next to it. To see what branches exist and which one you're on.

commands.title: List all branches
commands.description: Shows both local and remote-tracking branches. Remote branches are shown in red. To see all branches including ones on GitHub that you haven't checked out yet.

commands.title: Create + switch to new branch
commands.description: Creates a new branch from your current position and switches to it immediately. The modern way to create branches. Replace 'feature/login' with a descriptive name like 'fix/header-bug' or 'feature/dark-mode'. When starting work on a new feature, bug fix, or experiment. 💡

commands.title: Switch to existing branch
commands.description: Moves to an existing branch. Your files will change to match that branch's state. Replace 'main' with the branch name you want to switch to. When you want to work on a different branch. 💡

commands.title: Switch to previous branch
commands.description: Jumps back to whatever branch you were on before. Like the 'back' button on your browser. When you quickly switched to another branch and want to go back.

commands.title: Create branch from specific commit
commands.description: Creates a new branch starting from a specific commit instead of the current position. When you need to branch from a specific point in history.

commands.title: Rename current branch
commands.description: Changes the name of the branch you're currently on. When you mistyped a branch name or it no longer reflects the work.

commands.title: Rename any branch
commands.description: Renames a branch even if you're not on it. When you need to rename a branch you're not currently working on.

commands.title: Delete merged branch
commands.description: Safely deletes a branch that has been merged. Git will REFUSE to delete unmerged branches with this command. After a feature branch has been merged into main — cleanup time.

commands.title: Force-delete branch
commands.description: Deletes a branch even if it has unmerged commits. The commits may be lost forever! When you're 100% sure you want to discard the branch and all its work.

commands.title: Delete remote branch
commands.description: Removes a branch from GitHub (the remote). Does NOT delete your local copy. After merging a pull request — to clean up branches on GitHub.

commands.title: Check out detached commit
commands.description: Moves to a specific commit without being on any branch. Read-only inspection mode. When you want to look at the code at a specific point in history. 💡 Connect your local repo to GitHub and exchange commits. 'Origin' is the default name for your GitHub repo connection.

commands.title: Add remote (SSH)
commands.description: Connects your local repo to a GitHub repo under the name 'origin'. Use SSH URL for password-free pushes. Replace 'user/repo' with your GitHub username and repo name. After 'git init', before pushing for the first time.

commands.title: Add remote (HTTPS)
commands.description: Connects using HTTPS URL. You'll need to enter credentials or a personal access token. If you haven't set up SSH keys yet.

commands.title: List remotes
commands.description: Shows all configured remote connections with their URLs. You'll see fetch and push URLs. To verify which GitHub repo your local repo is connected to.

commands.title: Change remote URL
commands.description: "Updates the URL of an existing remote. Common use: switching from HTTPS to SSH." When the repo moved, or when switching from HTTPS to SSH after setting up keys.

commands.title: Remove a remote
commands.description: Disconnects the remote named 'origin'. Your local repo and files remain unchanged. When you want to disconnect from a repo and maybe connect to a different one.

commands.title: Fetch updates
commands.description: Downloads new commits from GitHub WITHOUT changing your files. Like checking for updates without installing them. To see what's new on GitHub before deciding to merge or rebase. 💡

commands.title: Fetch + cleanup
commands.description: Fetches updates and removes local references to branches that were deleted on GitHub. Periodically, to keep your branch list clean.

commands.title: Pull (fetch + merge)
commands.description: Downloads new commits from GitHub AND immediately merges them into your current branch. Make sure you're on the right branch first (check with 'git branch'). To bring your local branch up to date with what's on GitHub.

commands.title: Pull with rebase
commands.description: Pulls updates and replays your local commits on top. Creates a cleaner, linear history. Preferred when you have local commits that haven't been pushed yet. 💡

commands.title: Push current branch
commands.description: Uploads your commits to GitHub. Only works if the branch exists on GitHub already. After committing, to share your work with others (or save it as backup).

commands.title: Push + set upstream
commands.description: Pushes and links your local branch to the remote branch. After this, 'git push' and 'git pull' work without extra arguments. Replace 'main' with your branch name. Only needed once per branch. The FIRST time you push a brand-new branch to GitHub.

commands.title: Push new branch shortcut
commands.description: Pushes the current branch (whatever it's named) and sets up tracking. HEAD = 'whatever branch I'm on'. When you create a new branch and want to push it without typing the name. 💡

commands.title: Safe force-push
commands.description: Force-pushes but only if nobody else pushed to the branch since your last fetch. Safer than --force. After amending a commit or rebasing a branch you already pushed. 💡 Combine work from different branches. Merge preserves history; rebase rewrites it for a cleaner timeline.

commands.title: Merge branch into current
commands.description: Takes all commits from 'feature/login' and combines them into your current branch, creating a merge commit. 1. Switch to the branch you want to merge INTO (usually main) 2. Run 'git merge feature/login' 3. If no conflicts, it's done! When a feature is done and you want to bring it into 'main'.

commands.title: Merge with explicit commit
commands.description: Always creates a merge commit, even if Git could do a fast-forward. Preserves the fact that a branch existed. When you want the history to clearly show where a feature branch was merged.

commands.title: Squash merge
commands.description: Combines ALL commits from the branch into one staged changeset. You then commit manually with a clean message. 1. Run the command "2. Run 'git commit -m \"feat: add login feature\"'" All the branch's changes become one commit. When a branch has messy commits and you want one clean commit on main.

commands.title: Abort a merge
commands.description: Cancels an in-progress merge and returns everything to how it was before the merge started. When you hit conflicts you don't want to resolve right now.

commands.title: Rebase onto main
commands.description: Takes your branch's commits and replays them on top of main's latest commit. Creates a clean, linear history. 1. Make sure you're on your feature branch 2. Run 'git rebase main' 3. Your commits are now 'after' main's commits To update your feature branch with the latest changes from main. 💡

commands.title: Interactive rebase
commands.description: Opens an editor showing the last 5 commits. You can reorder, squash, edit, or delete them. "Change 5 to however many commits you want to edit. In the editor:" pick = keep, squash = merge into previous, drop = delete To clean up messy commit history before pushing or opening a pull request.

commands.title: Continue rebase after conflict
commands.description: Resumes a paused rebase after you've fixed conflicts and staged the resolved files. Mid-rebase, after fixing a conflict with 'git add'.

commands.title: Abort rebase
commands.description: Cancels the entire rebase and goes back to how everything was before. When a rebase gets too messy and you want to start over.

commands.title: Cherry-pick a commit
commands.description: Copies a specific commit from another branch and applies it to your current branch. Replace abc1234 with the commit hash (find it with 'git log --oneline'). When you need just one fix or feature from another branch without merging everything.

commands.title: Cherry-pick without committing
commands.description: Applies the commit's changes to your working tree but doesn't auto-commit. You can modify before committing. When you want to adjust the cherry-picked changes before committing.

commands.title: Resolve merge conflicts
commands.command: # In Acode: open the conflicted file, look for <<<<<<< markers
commands.description: When Git can't auto-merge, it marks conflicts in files with <<<<<<< (your changes), ======= (separator), and >>>>>>> (their changes). You manually choose what to keep. 1. Open conflicted file in Acode 2. Find the <<<<<<< markers 3. Keep the code you want, delete the markers 4. Save → 'git add file' → 'git merge --continue' or 'git rebase --continue' Whenever 'git merge' or 'git rebase' says CONFLICT. Explore your commit history, see what changed, and find who changed what and when.

commands.title: Pretty commit log
commands.description: Shows the last 20 commits in a compact, visual format with branch/merge lines and tag/branch labels. To get a quick overview of recent history. The most useful log format. 💡

commands.title: Full log (detailed)
commands.description: Shows full commit details — hash, author, date, and message. Press q to exit, space for next page. Press Space to scroll, q to quit. Use arrow keys to navigate. When you need full commit details.

commands.title: Log by author
commands.description: Filters commits by author and time range. Great for seeing what you've done recently. To review your own recent work or track someone else's contributions.

commands.title: Log for a specific file
commands.description: Shows every commit that touched a specific file, including the actual changes (diff). --follow tracks renames. When you want to see how a specific file evolved over time.

commands.title: Search commits by message
commands.description: Finds commits whose messages contain the search term. When you're looking for a commit about a specific feature or fix.

commands.title: Search commits by code change
commands.description: Finds commits where a specific string was added or removed from the code. When you want to find when a function/variable was introduced or removed.

commands.title: Show a specific commit
commands.description: Displays the full details and diff of one specific commit. When you want to see exactly what a particular commit changed.

commands.title: Show unstaged changes
commands.description: Shows line-by-line differences between your working files and what's staged/committed. Before 'git add' — to review what you're about to stage.

commands.title: Show staged changes
commands.description: Shows what's in the staging area — exactly what will go into the next commit. After 'git add', before 'git commit' — final review.

commands.title: Compare two branches
commands.description: Shows all differences between two branches. Before merging, to preview what changes the merge will bring.

commands.title: Who changed this line (blame)
commands.description: Shows who last modified each line of a file, with the commit hash and date. When investigating why a line of code exists or who wrote it.

commands.title: Reflog (safety net)
commands.description: Shows a log of EVERYTHING you've done — every checkout, commit, rebase, reset. Your ultimate undo history. When you think you've lost work after a reset, rebase, or other destructive operation. 💡

commands.title: Show file at specific commit
commands.description: Displays the contents of a file as it was at a specific commit, without changing your working tree. When you want to see an old version of a file without checking it out.

commands.title: Count commits per author
commands.description: Shows a summary of how many commits each author has made, sorted by count. For a quick overview of who contributed the most. Mistakes happen! Here's how to undo changes safely — or aggressively when needed.

commands.title: Discard ALL changes
commands.description: Reverts ALL modified files to the last committed state. DESTROYS all uncommitted work. Nuclear option — when you want everything back to how it was at the last commit.

commands.title: Unstage everything
commands.description: Removes all files from the staging area. Your edits are kept, just no longer staged. When you did 'git add .' by mistake and want to unstage everything.

commands.title: Delete untracked files (dry run)
commands.description: Shows which untracked files WOULD be deleted, without actually deleting them. Always do this first! Before running 'git clean -fd' — to preview what will be deleted.

commands.title: Delete untracked files
commands.description: Permanently removes all untracked files and empty directories. Cannot be undone! To clean up generated files, build artifacts, or accidentally created files.

commands.title: Revert a commit (safe)
commands.description: Creates a NEW commit that undoes the changes from a previous commit. History stays intact — safe for shared branches. Replace abc1234 with the commit hash to undo. Git creates a new 'reverse' commit. On shared branches (like main) where you must not rewrite history.

commands.title: Soft reset (undo commit, keep staged)
commands.description: Moves HEAD back one commit. Your changes are still staged and ready to re-commit. HEAD~1 = go back 1 commit. HEAD~3 = go back 3 commits. When you committed too early and want to modify what's in the commit.

commands.title: Mixed reset (undo commit, keep files)
commands.description: Moves HEAD back one commit. Changes are kept in your files but unstaged. When you want to re-stage files selectively before committing again.

commands.title: Hard reset (destroy everything)
commands.description: Moves HEAD back one commit and DELETES all changes since. Like it never happened. Only when you're 100% sure you want to permanently discard commits and all changes. 💡

commands.title: Reset to match remote
commands.description: Makes your local branch identical to what's on GitHub. Destroys all local changes and commits. When your local branch is messed up and you want a fresh copy from GitHub.

commands.title: Recover a deleted commit
commands.description: First lists all recent HEAD changes (reflog), then resets to the commit you want to recover. 1. Run 'git reflog' 2. Find the commit hash you want to recover 3. Run 'git reset --hard <hash>' After accidentally resetting or deleting commits. Temporarily save your work-in-progress without committing. Like a clipboard for your code changes.

commands.title: Stash changes
commands.description: Saves all your dirty (modified) files aside and gives you a clean working tree. The message helps you find it later. Replace the message with something descriptive. Your files go back to the last commit state. When you need to switch branches but aren't ready to commit your current work.

commands.title: Stash including new files
commands.command: git stash push -u -m \"wip: including new files\"
commands.description: Same as stash, but also includes untracked (brand new) files that aren't staged yet. When your work-in-progress includes new files you haven't 'git add'-ed. 💡

commands.title: Quick stash (no message)
commands.description: Stashes everything with an auto-generated message. Fast but harder to identify later. When you need to stash quickly and don't have time for a message.

commands.title: List stashes
commands.description: Shows all stashed entries with their index number and message. To see what you've stashed and pick which one to restore.

commands.title: Show stash contents
commands.description: Shows the actual code changes in a specific stash entry. To review what's in a stash before applying it.

commands.title: Pop latest stash
commands.description: Restores the most recent stash and removes it from the stash list. When you're back on the right branch and want to continue your work.

commands.title: Apply specific stash
commands.description: Restores a specific stash but keeps it in the stash list (can be re-applied later). When you might need to apply the same stash to multiple branches.

commands.title: Drop a stash
commands.description: Permanently deletes a specific stash entry. After confirming you no longer need that stashed work.

commands.title: Clear all stashes
commands.description: Deletes ALL stashes. Cannot be undone! Spring cleaning — when you want to remove all stashed entries. Mark specific commits as releases or milestones. Tags are permanent bookmarks in your history.

commands.title: Create annotated tag
commands.description: Creates a permanent, annotated tag with a message. Annotated tags include author, date, and message — preferred for releases. When cutting a release version of your project.

commands.title: Create lightweight tag
commands.description: Creates a simple tag without extra metadata. Just a pointer to a commit. For quick, informal markers. Use annotated tags for real releases.

commands.title: Tag a past commit
commands.description: Tags a specific commit in the past, not the current one. When you forgot to tag a commit at the time and want to add it retroactively.

commands.title: List all tags
commands.description: Lists all tags in the repo. To see existing release markers.

commands.title: Show tag details
commands.description: Shows the tag message, author, date, and the commit it points to. To inspect what a specific tag refers to.

commands.title: Push a tag
commands.description: Uploads a specific tag to GitHub. Tags are NOT pushed automatically with 'git push'. After creating a release tag — to publish it on GitHub.

commands.title: Push all tags
commands.description: Pushes every local tag to GitHub at once. When syncing many tags at once.

commands.title: Delete a local tag
commands.description: Removes a tag from your local repo. Does NOT remove it from GitHub. When a tag was created by mistake.

commands.title: Delete a remote tag
commands.description: Removes a tag from GitHub. When you need to remove a tag that was pushed by mistake. Control which files Git should ignore. Essential for keeping secrets, build files, and junk out of your repo.

commands.title: Ignore node_modules
commands.description: Adds node_modules/ to .gitignore. This folder can be hundreds of MB — NEVER commit it. At the start of any JavaScript/Node.js project.

commands.title: Ignore environment files
commands.description: Prevents .env files (which contain secrets like API keys and passwords) from being committed. ALWAYS. Never commit .env files — they contain sensitive data. 💡

commands.title: Ignore build outputs
commands.description: Ignores common build/output directories. These are generated and shouldn't be in the repo. For projects that have a build step (React, Next.js, etc.).

commands.title: Ignore OS files
commands.description: Ignores operating system junk files (macOS, Windows, vim swap files). At the start of every project — these files are useless in Git.

commands.title: Ignore log files
commands.description: Ignores log files which can grow large and aren't useful in version control. For any project that generates log files.

commands.title: Check why a file is ignored
commands.description: Shows which .gitignore rule is causing a specific file to be ignored. When a file you want to track is being ignored and you can't figure out why.

commands.title: Stop tracking ignored file
commands.command: git rm --cached path/to/file && git commit -m 'chore: remove tracked file'
commands.description: Removes a file from Git tracking but keeps it on disk. Use after adding it to .gitignore. When you accidentally committed a file that should be ignored.

commands.title: Global gitignore
commands.description: Sets a global .gitignore that applies to ALL repos on your device. To always ignore OS files (.DS_Store, Thumbs.db) across all projects.

commands.title: Sync fork with upstream
commands.command: git fetch upstream && git rebase upstream/main && git push
commands.description: Fetches latest changes from the original repo and updates your fork. Periodically, to keep your fork up to date with the original project.

commands.title: Create a PR-ready branch
commands.command: git switch -c fix/issue-42 && # make changes && git add . && git commit -m \"fix: resolve issue #42\" && git push -u origin HEAD
commands.description: "Complete workflow: create branch → make changes → commit → push. Now go to GitHub to create the Pull Request." Whenever you want to contribute a fix or feature via Pull Request.

commands.title: Create GitHub repo from Termux
commands.description: GitHub repos must be created on the website first. After that, connect your local repo to it. 1. Go to github.com → New Repository 2. Name it, DON'T initialize with README 3. Copy the SSH URL "4. In Termux: git remote add origin <URL>" 5. git push -u origin main When starting a new project you want on GitHub.

commands.title: Create personal access token
commands.command: # GitHub → Settings → Developer Settings → Tokens → Generate
commands.description: If using HTTPS, you need a Personal Access Token instead of your password. It's like a temporary password for Git. 1. GitHub.com → Settings → Developer settings 2. Personal access tokens → Tokens (classic) 3. Generate new token → select 'repo' scope 4. Copy the token — use it as your password If you don't use SSH and Git asks for a password when pushing.

commands.title: Find the bad commit (bisect)
commands.command: git bisect start && git bisect bad && git bisect good abc1234
commands.description: Binary search through commit history to find exactly which commit introduced a bug. Git checks out commits for you to test. 1. Start bisect 2. Mark current (broken) as bad 3. Mark a known-good commit 4. Git checks out middle commit → test it → 'git bisect good' or 'git bisect bad' 5. Repeat until Git finds the culprit 6. 'git bisect reset' when done When a bug appeared and you need to find which commit caused it.

commands.title: Worktree (work on 2 branches)
commands.description: Creates a separate folder where another branch is checked out. Work on two branches at the same time! When you need to fix a bug on main without losing your feature branch work.

commands.title: Sparse checkout
commands.command: git sparse-checkout init --cone && git sparse-checkout set src docs
commands.description: Downloads only specific folders from a large repo instead of everything. Working with huge monorepos where you only need certain directories.

commands.title: Add a submodule
commands.description: Embeds another Git repo as a subdirectory at a specific commit. When your project depends on another repo's source code.

commands.title: Git LFS (large files)
commands.command: git lfs install && git lfs track "*.psd"
commands.description: Installs Git Large File Storage for handling big binary files (images, videos, designs). When your repo needs to store large binary files without bloating history.

commands.title: Archive a branch
commands.description: Creates a zip file of your repo at a specific branch/tag without the .git history. When you need to share or deploy code as a zip file.

commands.title: Count lines of code
commands.description: Counts total lines across all tracked files in the repo. For fun stats about your project size.

commands.title: Garbage collect
commands.description: Cleans up unnecessary files and optimizes the repo. Frees disk space. Occasionally, on repos that feel slow. Or after removing large files from history. The most essential commands for daily use. If you remember nothing else, remember these!

commands.title: Daily workflow (complete)
commands.command: git pull && git add . && git commit -m \"feat: your message\" && git push
commands.description: "The complete daily workflow: get latest changes → stage your work → commit → push to GitHub." 1. git pull (get latest) 2. Make your changes in Acode 3. git add . (stage everything) 4. git commit -m 'message' (save snapshot) 5. git push (upload to GitHub) This is the bread and butter — the commands you'll use every single day.

commands.title: New feature workflow
commands.command: git switch -c feature/name && # code && git add . && git commit -m \"feat: description\" && git push -u origin HEAD
commands.description: "Complete workflow for building a new feature: create branch → code → commit → push → then create PR on GitHub." Every time you start working on something new.

commands.title: Oops, undo last commit
commands.description: "Quick undo: removes the last commit but keeps all your changes staged. Easy to re-commit." When you just committed and immediately realize you need to change something.

commands.title: What just happened?
commands.description: Shows the last 10 commits as one-liners. Quick way to see recent history. When you want to quickly check what's been going on.

commands.title: Am I on the right branch?
commands.description: Shows just the name of the current branch. Nothing else. Quick check before committing or pushing.

commands.title: What files did I change?
commands.description: "Ultra-compact status: one letter + filename per line. M=modified, A=added, ??=untracked, D=deleted." Quick glance at what's changed without verbose output.

commands.title: Clone a repository
commands.description: Downloads a full copy of a repository to your local machine. Replace username/repo with the actual GitHub path. Use git@ (SSH) if you've set up keys, or https:// if not. Every time you want to work on an existing GitHub project.

commands.title: Clone a repo (HTTPS)
commands.description: Downloads a complete copy of a remote repository including all history, branches, and files. 1. Go to the repo on GitHub 2. Click the green 'Code' button 3. Copy the HTTPS URL 4. In Termux, navigate to your projects folder 5. Run 'git clone <URL>' When you want to work on an existing project from GitHub.

commands.title: Clone a repo (SSH)
commands.description: Clones using SSH — no password needed if you've set up SSH keys. Preferred over HTTPS. After setting up SSH keys — this is the easiest way to clone. 💡

commands.title: Clone into specific folder
commands.description: Clones the repo but puts it in a folder named 'my-project' instead of the repo name. When you want a custom folder name for the cloned repo.

commands.title: Shallow clone (fast)
commands.description: Downloads only the latest snapshot — no history. Much faster and uses less data. Perfect for mobile! When you just need the latest code and don't care about commit history. Great for saving mobile data. 💡

commands.title: Clone a specific branch
commands.description: Downloads only one specific branch instead of all branches. Saves bandwidth. When you only need one branch and want to save time and data. Track changes and save snapshots to history. Think of staging as 'selecting files for a photo' and committing as 'taking the photo'.

commands.title: Fork + clone workflow
commands.command: git clone git@github.com:YOUR-USERNAME/repo.git && cd repo && git remote add upstream git@github.com:ORIGINAL-OWNER/repo.git
commands.description: "The standard open-source contribution workflow: fork on GitHub, clone your fork, add the original repo as 'upstream'." 1. Fork the repo on GitHub (click Fork button) 2. Clone YOUR fork 3. Add the original as 'upstream' for syncing When contributing to someone else's project on GitHub.

commands.title: Init + update submodules
commands.description: Clones and checks out all submodules after cloning a repo that uses them. After cloning a repo that contains submodules.

commands.title: Clone a repository
commands.description: Downloads an existing GitHub repository to your local machine and automatically configures the remote connection. Replace user/repo with the actual repository path. When starting work on an existing project or contributing to someone else's codebase.

commands.title: Clone into a custom folder
commands.description: Clones a repository and stores it inside a folder with a custom name instead of the repository name. Replace my-project with your preferred folder name. Useful when organizing multiple projects or avoiding naming conflicts.

commands.title: Clone a specific branch
commands.description: Clones only the specified branch and checks it out immediately. Replace develop with the branch name you want. Useful when you only need a feature branch or staging branch instead of the default branch.

commands.title: Show branch tracking info
commands.description: Displays all local branches along with their upstream tracking branches and ahead/behind status. Helps you see which branches are connected to GitHub and whether they need to be pushed or pulled.

commands.title: Show current branch
commands.description: Displays only the name of the branch you're currently working on. Faster than viewing the full branch list when you just need to confirm your current branch.

commands.title: Show remote details
commands.description: Displays detailed information about the origin remote, including fetch and push URLs, tracked branches, and the default branch. Useful for troubleshooting remote repository connections.

commands.title: Show remote branches
commands.description: Lists all branches that currently exist on the remote repository without fetching them locally. Useful when checking available branches on GitHub.

commands.title: Show changed filenames
commands.description: Displays only the names of files that have changed, without showing the actual code differences. Useful for quickly reviewing affected files before committing.

commands.title: Show staged filenames
commands.description: Lists only the files currently staged for the next commit. Useful for verifying what will be included before running git commit.

commands.title: Show files changed between branches
commands.description: Displays all files that differ between two branches. Replace the branch names as needed. Useful before merging to see which files will be affected.

commands.title: Restore file from another branch
commands.description: Replaces a file in your current branch with the version from another branch. Replace main and the file path as needed. Useful when you want to recover a file without switching branches.

commands.title: Restore file from a commit
commands.description: Restores a file exactly as it existed in a specific commit. Replace abc1234 with the commit hash. Useful for recovering an older version of a file without affecting the rest of the project.

commands.title: Create branch from stash
commands.description: Creates a new branch and immediately applies a stash to it. This is the safest way to continue stashed work without affecting your current branch.

commands.title: Stash a single file
commands.description: Stashes changes from a specific file instead of the entire working directory. Useful when you only want to temporarily set aside one file while continuing work on others.

commands.title: Git garbage collection
commands.description: Optimizes the repository by cleaning up unnecessary files and compressing Git objects. Helps improve repository performance and reduce storage usage.

commands.title: Verify repository integrity
commands.description: Checks the repository for corruption, missing objects, and structural problems. Useful when troubleshooting repository issues or after recovering lost history.

commands.title: Check why a file is ignored
commands.description: Shows exactly which .gitignore rule is causing a file to be ignored. Useful when Git refuses to track a file and you need to find the matching ignore pattern.

commands.title: Create status alias
commands.description: Creates a shortcut so you can type 'git st' instead of 'git status'. Useful for speeding up everyday Git workflows.

commands.title: Create pretty log alias
commands.description: Creates a shortcut command called 'git lg' that displays a compact visual representation of your repository history with branches and merges.

commands.title: Show files changed in last commit
commands.description: Displays the most recent commit along with the files it changed. Useful for quickly reviewing what was included in your last commit.

commands.title: Recover a deleted branch
commands.command: git reflog && git branch recovered-branch abc1234
commands.description: Uses reflog to find lost commits and recreates a branch pointing to a recovered commit. Replace abc1234 with the commit hash found in reflog. Useful after accidentally deleting a branch.

commands.title: Remove file from all history
commands.description: Rewrites ENTIRE history to remove a file from every commit. Use when you accidentally committed secrets. "Emergency: when API keys, passwords, or sensitive files were committed." 💡
